catalog_numbers_correct.claim: 7.66x TTFT on Llama-3.1-405B-FP8 by pruning the prompt
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: 7.66x at 10% kept, batch x seq up to 16x32K, 8x H200, vs unpruned 405B
H100 for quality, H200 for efficiency runs
Multi-Doc QA only

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: first-pass: aggregation tasks degrade at 10% keep
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Table 2 aggregation column (CWE/FWE) at 10% keep: 77.9 vs full-prompt 99.7 at 4K, 70.0 vs 96.9 at 32K; the average column excludes aggregation

why: The prune-the-prompt idea transfers; the 7.66x does not. (1) GPU TP8 where prefill is compute-bound, so cost falls ~linearly with kept tokens (paper: 'reduces total FLOPS proportional to the percentage of token drop'); on NVMe-streamed experts, a 500-token prefill touches most experts anyway, so bytes saturate and our own bound is 1.48x/1.80x/2.77x at 50/25/12.5% kept (F.md). (2) The speculator is an 8B dense model run over the FULL prompt first; its overhead is 2% of a 405B but 8B dense = ~16 GFLOP/token vs ~12 GFLOP/token active for the 125B MoE (my arithmetic from F.md's 12 GFLOP), so on our target the speculator would cost MORE compute than the target; a 0.6-1.7B speculator (as in P-0245) is needed, and its RAM competes with 8-32 GB. (3) Batch of 16-128 sequences, speedups grow with batch*seq. (4) Needs the speculator resident plus 2-pass logic; no multi-turn recompute (stated limitation).
quality_loss: Lossy. LongBench 70B: 98.5% of baseline at 10% kept, 100.7% at 30% (Table 1). RULER at 10% kept: aggregation tasks drop (CWE/FWE 77.9 vs 99.7 at 4K); standard short tasks degrade at low keep rate because prompts are information dense (Appendix Fig 6, text Sec 4.6). No perplexity/logit outputs (cannot score prompt tokens).
ablation: Variants SpecPrefill / Full / Full+look-ahead (Fig 2, Fig 8), keep-rate sweep, batch x seq sweep (Fig 3/4), vs MInference (Fig 5: 2.54x-6.54x relative speedup). Nothing isolating I/O or MoE.
limitations: Stated (Sec 5): no explicit logits for all input tokens, so only generative evaluation; multi-turn conversations can fail without KV recompute; need a better method to choose how many tokens to keep; aggregation tasks are information-dense.
contradicts_our_findings: No contradiction. It supports our F.md statement that prompt pruning only pays when compute (not bytes) scales with tokens; the paper's 7.66x is within 1% of its own FLOP-ratio bound (7.72x), i.e. it is a pure compute-scaling result. Our 'bytes saturate' bound for MoE-from-disk is a regime the paper never tests.

contradicts_our_findings: None. Does not report any MoE-specific cost; DeepSeek-V3 is MoE but resident in RDU memory.

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: our own 4.4-6.0x re-read figure vs this paper
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: paper measures total expert loads (prefill+decode, 100 requests, GPU HBM) = 1.64x on arXiv with ~18 chunks per prompt; our 4.4-6.0x is prefill-only, 8 chunks of 64 tokens, on a tiny cache (F.md). Not comparable, not a contradiction

why: Directionally yes (the mechanism, redundant expert reloads per token chunk, is precisely the cost that dominates NVMe streaming), but all numbers are for GPU HBM-resident experts with concurrent requests, 512-token chunks, SLO-bound TBT and decode batches of 32-128. Batch-1 laptop prefill has no decode to interleave with, so the 'stall-free' goal does not exist; the useful kernel is simply 'for a prompt, process layer-major (all tokens through layer l, read each expert once) instead of token-chunk-major', i.e. our expert-major prefill idea (B.md #9). Assumptions that break: GPU, batch>1, SLO scheduling; the paper does not use disk or CPU.
ablation: Group-size Nlg sweep (Table 11: Nlg 2/4/8/16 TTFT 0.48/0.57/0.77/1.27 s, p99 TBT 138/84.5/54.6/35.7 ms); dense-model control (slower); disaggregated serving comparison (Table 10: TTFT 3.00 chunked, 3.94 disaggregated, 1.24 layered); relaxed-TBT convergence (chunk 2048 == Nlg 4, TTFT 2.47 s both). Closest to isolating the 'redundant reload' cost.
limitations: Conclusion: multi-GPU extension and adaptive layer grouping are future work; the gain vanishes with large chunks (relaxed SLO) and is negative for dense models; layer count must divide into groups.
contradicts_our_findings: No contradiction; supports our 'token-chunked prefill re-reads experts' finding qualitatively. The magnitude (1.64x) is much lower than our 4.4-6.0x because their chunks are 8x larger (512 vs 64) and loads include decode.

Table 4 values imply our f=0.107 for prose is near the paper's ShareGPT/GSM8K regime (1.4-2.0 tokens per step incl. bonus), i.e. accepted drafts 0.4-1.0 per step, a higher acceptance than our stand-in prose corpus (0.11). Mild: our stand-in corpora (Python docs) may under-estimate real chat overlap.

why: Direction transfers strongly (verify cost grows with the union of experts; this is our F.md pass-cost curve). Numbers do not: all are single-request or large-batch GPU runs with all experts in HBM (MoE-Spec, EVICT) or CPU-RAM-offloaded with large batches and Mixtral's 8 experts (SpecMoEOff), 1B-47B models, EAGLE-class trained drafts (not n-gram). MoE-Spec is LOSSY (drops tail experts; ~5% quality loss at 2x on Qwen3, 22% on Mixtral at max budget). EVICT is lossless and the more relevant remedy: for an n-gram draft the analogous rule is 'truncate the draft when the marginal expert-union cost exceeds the expected gain', which our measured pass-cost curve can feed. Cache size as share of experts (not modelled by any of them) breaks the transfer.
quality_loss: MoE-Spec: lossy, task metrics within one std of EAGLE at the chosen budget (Table 1), but ~95% (Qwen3) to ~78% (Mixtral) of AR quality at aggressive budgets; sampling at T=1 inherits EAGLE's q(x)=1 distribution shift (footnote 3). EVICT: lossless. SpecMoEOff: lossless verification.
ablation: MoE-Spec: selection method (router vs oracle vs others), coverage policy, token policy (truncation vs substitution), tree size and budget sweeps (Sec 4.4-4.5). EVICT: adaptive prefix vs fixed. No ablation with an SSD tier or an LRU expert cache.
limitations: MoE-Spec (Sec 6): budget hyperparameter per deployment; single-request A100 only; gains may shrink with batch; softmax routing only (DeepSeek-V3 sigmoid routing needs adaptation); no per-layer budgets. EVICT: SGLang eager mode shows slight regression from the extra runtime ops.
contradicts_our_findings: No. Consistent with F.md (0.40->1.79 s per verify pass at 8 GB). One refinement: MoE-Spec shows saturation at ~32 of 64 experts yields most of the speedup (a long tail of rarely-used experts), which suggests a cap on experts per verify pass is a cheaper lever than shortening drafts; we have not measured it on our traces.

why: Dense 7-8B models resident on an RTX 4090, batch 1, 80-item benchmarks with long retrieved contexts (high overlap by construction); the trie proposes MULTIPLE branch drafts verified with tree attention, which on a streamed MoE multiplies the expert union per verify pass (the MoE-Spec / Cascade effect). Overlap requirement same as P-0251; gain collapses with noisy retrieval (0.65x of clean) and on Llama-3 summarization (1.06x). Assumptions broken: GPU, dense weights, tree verification cost not modelled.

limitations: Sec 6: ties in frequency scores prune useful drafts under the fixed num_draft; strong dependence on quality of retrieved corpora (noisy retrieval hurts); n, Lp need tuning per model/dataset; timing noisy because GPU was shared (Appendix).
